headline: South Africa votes. The ANC may have its worst day ever.
summary: South Africans voted Wednesday for the councils that run nearly 300 municipalities: water, electricity, rubbish. The ANC, in charge since apartheid ended in 1994, took 70% of the vote in 2004 and 40% at the last national election. One poll puts it at 30% now, down from 46% in the 2021 local vote. Ramaphosa says it is going higher.

cover_question.q: Why don't people like them anymore?

cover_answer: Rubbish in the streets and no water on Mondays.
table_question: If a job gets done badly for years, do you fire them or help?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: In Soweto, in South Africa, a man told the BBC his water stops every Monday afternoon. Today grown-ups there voted on who runs their towns: the water, the lights and the rubbish trucks. One team has run things for 32 years, and many want someone new, like a class picking a new line leader. Our taps are fine, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: A dry tap on a Monday is a thing they can picture. The vote is a line leader.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script starts at a tap that runs dry on Monday afternoons, a thing they can test at the sink. A country they cannot place is beyond them; the line-leader vote is a rule they have used. Expect "why does the water stop?" Nobody in charge has fixed it, so there is a vote.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: South Africa's towns are run by councils that handle water, power and rubbish. The auditor found only 39 of 257 with clean books, and Johannesburg has been called bankrupt. Voters can fire a council the way a team votes out a captain who never shows up. The ANC: 70% in 2004, maybe 30% now.
8-12.why: Clean books, a bankrupt city, a vote: one chain. They want to see a rule enforced, and firing the captain is one they know.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect and whether rules get applied, so the script hands them a chain: a council's job, an audit it failed, a vote that can remove it. The captain who never shows up is a rule they have enforced themselves. Expect "who do they vote for instead?" Over 500 parties, and the BBC says one is gaining.

13-17.script: If things have got worse for years, is voting the fix or a wasted morning? In Alexandra an 18-year-old told the BBC he will vote for the first time; most of his friends never registered. Second: Africa's richest square mile, Sandton, is a short walk from Alexandra's potholes. What would you tell the friends?
13-17.why: Two neighbours, two answers to the same potholes. Let them pick first.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: a vote that changed little for years, and a vote as the only lever a resident has. The script gives them an 18-year-old and a 33-year-old in one township who chose differently, and asks them to argue it. Expect "would you vote there?" Say what you would do, and let them push back.

5-7.q: Why do they vote about rubbish?
5-7.a: They pick who runs the trucks, water and lights. If those stop, pick someone else.

8-12.q: Why don't people like them anymore?
8-12.a: Rubbish piles, water cuts, power cuts, and anger over corruption.
In charge since apartheid ended in 1994. 70% in 2004, maybe 30% now.

13-17.q: If nothing changes, why bother voting?
13-17.a: One Soweto man with no water on Mondays is voting. His neighbour isn't.

13-17.q: Why did people vote ANC for 30 years, then?
13-17.a: It won 70% in 2004. Corruption, joblessness and crime wore that down.
